Magnetic correlations in the S​U​(3)SU(3) triangular-lattice tt-JJ model at finite doping

Annika Böhler Affiliation: Department of Physics and Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics (ASC), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, München D-80333, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology, Schellingstr. 4, Munich D-80799, Germany    Fabian Grusdt Affiliation: Department of Physics and Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics (ASC), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, München D-80333, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology, Schellingstr. 4, Munich D-80799, Germany    Annabelle Bohrdt Affiliation: Department of Physics and Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics (ASC), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, München D-80333, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology, Schellingstr. 4, Munich D-80799, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Ultracold alkaline-earth atoms and molecules now enable experimental realizations of SU(N)-symmetric Fermi-Hubbard models, yet theoretical understanding of these systems, particularly at finite doping remains limited. Here we investigate the strong-coupling limit of the S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetric Fermi-Hubbard model on the triangular lattice across the full doping range. Using a three-flavor extension of Gutzwiller-projected hidden fermion determinant states (G-HFDS), a neural network based variational ansatz, we analyze two- and three-point spin-spin and spin-spin-hole correlations of the S​U​(3)SU(3) Cartan generators. We further study the structure of a pair of doped holes for large periodic systems, and compare our results to the paradigmatic S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice equivalent, finding strikingly similar magnetic correlations, non-s-wave pairing symmetry, and enhanced binding energies. Our results provide a foundation for future exploration of doped SU(N) Mott insulators, providing valuable insights for both theoretical developments and quantum simulation experiments.

Introduction. The Fermi-Hubbard (FH) model plays a central role in understanding the physics of doped Mott insulators (MI), and has been extensively studied both numerically [1, 41, 35, 51, 67] and experimentally [8]. At weak coupling, these systems can often be approached using perturbative methods, offering a controlled understanding of ordering phenomena [52, 37]. However, key features such as magnetism, pairing, and pseudogap physics arise from strongly entangled degrees of freedom in the strong coupling regime. The need for a universal approach to strongly coupled systems motivates extensions to higher S​U​(N>2)SU(N>2) spin symmetries, which offer a controlled framework for disentangling the specific features of S​U​(2)SU(2) physics from more general aspects of strong couplings. S​U​(N)SU(N) versions of the FH model, relevant for ultra-cold atoms [12, 32] and multi-orbital materials [64, 44], reveal a rich variety of emergent phenomena beyond the physics of the S​U​(2)SU(2) systems [2, 28, 33, 61].

Experimental advances have enabled the realization of S​U​(N)SU(N) symmetric FH models using ultracold alkaline-earth atoms [32]. These experiments have observed Mott insulating states and magnetic correlations in S​U​(N=3,4,6)SU(N=3,4,6) FH models [66, 63, 26, 50, 62, 10, 45]. Recent experimental progress further allows the study of S​U​(N)SU(N) symmetric systems with ultracold molecules, enabling an even broader class of symmetries up to S​U​(N=36)SU(N=36), due to their rich internal structure [46]. While at unit filling ⟨n^i⟩=1\langle\hat{n}_{i}\rangle=1 and large UU, S​U​(N)SU(N) Heisenberg models have been shown to reveal intricate magnetic orders [65, 48, 3, 25, 47, 18], finite doping studies of these models remain limited [58, 20, 34].

In this work we employ a neural quantum state (NQS) ansatz [11] to study the strong coupling limit of the S​U​(3)SU(3) Fermi Hubbard model. Hereby, the wavefunction is parameterized as a neural network (NN), leveraging its universal function approximation capabilities [29]. The ability to approximate the ground state wave function has been successfully applied to areas challenging for traditional methods, such as frustrated spin systems [54, 14, 57], volume-law entangled states [60, 19, 43] and more recently also fermionic and bosonic systems [40, 49, 56, 39, 55, 15, 24].

We argue that the S​U​(3)SU(3) triangular lattice shares key physical features with the paradigmatic S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice, such as the existence of a three-flavor Neel state at zero doping that breaks the S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry. The elementary charge carriers of both models are described by magnetic polarons, and we compare the evolution of polaron correlations for the full doping range across both systems, providing microscopic explanations in terms of geometric strings [17, 22]. We further analyze pairing energies and symmetries of a pair of holes in the S​U​(3)SU(3) model and find enhanced pairing compared to the S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice case.

Model and Neural Network Ansatz. We study the strong coupling limit of the S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetric FH model, the S​U​(3)SU(3) tt-JJ model

H^t​JS​U​(3)=−t∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩𝒫^∑α(c^𝐢​α†c^𝐣​α+h.c.)𝒫^+J2∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩𝒫^(∑α,β(c^𝐢​α†c^𝐢​βc^𝐣​β†c^𝐣​α)−n^𝐢n^𝐣)𝒫^,\displaystyle\begin{split}\hat{H}^{SU(3)}_{tJ}=&-t\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\rangle}\hat{\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\alpha}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{j}\alpha}+h.c.\right)\hat{\mathcal{P}}\\ &+\frac{J}{2}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\rangle}\hat{\mathcal{P}}\left(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}\beta}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{j}\beta}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{j}\alpha}\right)-\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{j}}\right)\hat{\mathcal{P}},\end{split} (1)

on the triangular lattice, where the sum over α\alpha runs over three spin flavors, here represented by red, green and blue, see Fig. 1a. The local particle number is given as n^𝐢=∑αn^𝐢​α\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i}}=\sum_{\alpha}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i}\alpha} and ⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩\langle\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\rangle denotes nearest neighbors on the triangular lattice. 𝒫^=∏i∏⟨α,β⟩(1−n^i​α​n^i​β)\hat{\mathcal{P}}=\prod_{i}\prod_{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle}(1-\hat{n}_{i\alpha}\hat{n}_{i\beta}) represents a Gutzwiller projection onto maximally singly occupied sites, where ⟨α,β⟩\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle represents pairs of flavors.

At unit filling, the model maps to the S​U​(3)SU(3)-symmetric Heisenberg model, whose ground state has been shown both numerically and analytically to exhibit three-sublattice (3-SL) order on both square and triangular lattices [65, 3]. Contrary to the S​U​(2)SU(2) triangular lattice the S​U​(3)SU(3) model does not exhibit geometric frustration. At zero doping, the ground state is an S​U​(3)SU(3) symmetry-breaking antiferromagnet, described by the three-flavor Néel state, in close analogy to its counterpart on the S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice [9]. This is to be contrasted with the S​U​(3)SU(3) square lattice case, where a macroscopic ground state degeneracy prohibits the existence of a classical Néel state, making it numerically intractable without a priori inducing the correct symmetry breaking [4, 58]. In the low-doping limit of the AFM, the elementary charge carriers of both models can be described as magnetic polarons, consisting of doped charges dressed by a cloud of spin excitations.

In this study, we use of an NN ansatz with a hidden fermion construction [55]. We use a feed-forward neural network (FFNN) with a single hidden layer to represent the hidden fermion part of the ansatz, and impose an additional symmetrization over all possible spin permutations, i.e. ψ⁡(s)=∑g∈S3detM⁡(g​s)\psi(s)=\sum_{g\in S_{3}}\det M(gs), where S3S_{3} is the permutation group over the three spin flavors. The network is then trained by Monte Carlo sampling from the network distribution and updating the weights, using a variant of stochastic reconfiguration [13], such that the energy is minimized. We further employ a Gutzwiller projection in the sampling procedure, which has been shown to speed up convergence for the S​U​(2)SU(2) tt-JJ-model [39]. We choose a Gutzwiller projected Fermi sea as the initial state, which at unit filling represents the exact ground state in the S​U​(N→∞)SU(N\rightarrow\infty) limit [36]. We compare our results to matrix product state (MPS) calculations [30, 31] in an open boundary system up to 9×99\times 9 lattice sites, and find good agreement or even a slight advantage of the NQS method, see SM [59]. In the following, we will always focus on fully periodic systems, where MPS with their inherently one-dimensional structure become prohibitively expensive.

We see the same 3-SL pattern for both reference sites, confirming the overall 3-SL order of the ground state.

Next we study the evolution of magnetic correlations upon hole-doping δ=nh/L\delta=n_{h}/L for t/J=3t/J=3. Fig. 2b shows the magnitude of the nearest neighbor (nn) and next-nearest neighbor (nnn) correlations for different dopings. The cartoon inset shows the specific distances considered, which correspond to nn sites on different sublattices, and nnn sites on the same sublattice, showing the expected FM and AFM correlations of the 3-SL order in the low-doping regime. We observe that upon doping the correlations decrease, with the nnn correlations going through a sign change at δ≈0.25\delta\approx 0.25. The inset also show a comparison with the analogous nn and nnn correlations on the S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice from Ref. [39], which we find to be strikingly similar, highlighting the aforementioned analogy between the two models. We find that the sign crossing happens at similar doping values, indicating that the magnetic polaron regime and AFM region of the phase diagram have a similar dependence on doping as in the S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice case. Note that the sign change in the S​U​(3)SU(3) case is less pronounced, as expected from the fact that the maximal nn AFM correlations are smaller than in the S​U​(2)SU(2) case. The origin of the sign change and shape of the correlations can be explained within the geometric string theory developed for the S​U​(2)SU(2) Hubbard model, see next section.

To further investigate the effect of hole doping on the AFM order, we also study higher-order magnetic polaron correlations. In analogy to the S​U​(2)SU(2) case [39, 38], we define the connected correlations

The distances considered are shown in the cartoon inset, and we average over all equivalent configurations of sites around the hole. However, despite the qualitative agreement, we also observe a significant change in the amplitude of the connected correlations in the S​U​(3)SU(3) case. This quantitative change can again be understood from the microscopic string picture.

Comparison to Geometric String Theory. To provide a microscopic explanation of the observed magnetic correlations, we compare our results to the geometric string theory developed in the S​U​(2)SU(2) framework [23, 7, 22, 27, 6]. In this setting, the theory has yielded key insights into doped charge carriers and laid the groundwork for a cuprate pairing mechanism based on a Feshbach resonance. Extending and testing this theory in more general settings is therefore essential. Within the frozen spin approximation (FSA), where slow spin dynamics (∝J)(\propto J) are neglected relative to faster hole motion (∝t)(\propto t), doped holes in the low-doping regime generate geometric strings. Upon moving through the AFM background, a hole creates a string of displaced spins, see Fig. 2a. This provides a microscopic explanation for the sign change in the nn and nnn correlations: spin displacements along the string effectively flip FM and AFM bonds, mixing correlations and reversing the nnn amplitude.

The theory can be extended by analyzing hole motion in a frozen three-flavor AFM (Fig. 2a). As in the S​U​(2)SU(2) case, we observe a sign change in the two-point correlations for the same reason. However, in S​U​(3)SU(3) the shorter correlation range—due to the normalization of the Gell-Mann matrices—reduces the negative mixing contribution, making the sign change less pronounced. The change in the amplitude of the connected S​U​(2)SU(2) and S​U​(3)SU(3) correlations in Fig. 2c is likewise explained by string effects on neighboring bonds. Due to the higher connectivity of the triangular lattice and the additional flavors, the fraction of overall bonds whose configuration changes due to the hole motion from aligned to anti-aligned and vice versa is only 2/62/6, while 2/42/4 bonds are affected in the S​U​(2)SU(2) case. This smaller effect of the hole motion on the overall order of the spin background is reflected by the fact that the connected correlations are significantly smaller in the S​U​(3)SU(3) case. To make the comparison quantitative, we compute correlator expectation values within geometric string theory. Starting from undoped snapshots, we introduce holes with strings of displaced spins. The string-length distribution p⁡(l)p(l) is obtained by mapping the single-hole problem to a semi-infinite 1D model (see SM [59]). At finite doping, we add the required number of holes, assigning each a string with length drawn from p⁡(l)p(l), and evaluate the correlators as in Eq. (3). The predicted nn correlations agree well with the NQS results (see Fig. 2b), while deviations appear in the nnn correlator at intermediate doping.

Pair Structure and Binding Energies. One of the central open questions in the physics of cuprate superconductors is the microscopic mechanism of pairing. As a first step to study potential pairing in the S​U​(3)SU(3) model, we turn to an exploration of the two-hole structure. Due to the spin imbalance, we do not enforce the spin permutation symmetry in the NQS and work in a sector with fixed magnetization.

We start by analyzing the binding energies EB=E2​h−2​E1​hE_{B}=E_{2h}-2E_{1h}, for different parameters t/Jt/J. Here, E1​hE_{1h} and E2​hE_{2h} represent the energies of the single-hole and two-hole states relative to the undoped Néel state. The results are shown in Fig 3a. We find a negative binding energy EB<0E_{B}<0, the magnitude of which decreases as t/Jt/J is increased. This indicates that the doped charge carriers can lower their energy by binding together. Upon comparison, we find the amplitude of the binding energies to be larger than in the S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice case, where our NQS results are further confirmed by large-scale density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) studies, which reveal binding energies on the order of 0.2​t0.2t at t/J=2t/J=2 [5] and exact diagonalization studies showing a zero crossing at similar values of t/Jt/J [16, 42]. This large binding energy is especially surprising from a conventional BCS perspective, where the larger connectivity zz of the triangular lattice results in a smaller effective electron mass, which in turn indicates a smaller superconducting gap Δ\Delta and pairing energy of the Cooper pairs. However, in the geometric string picture, the increased binding energies can be explained by a geometric spinon-chargon repulsion, which increases with zz, favoring bound states at higher connectivity [23, 7], see SM [59].

We further investigate the distribution of distances between two doped holes available directly from the Monte Carlo snapshots, as shown in Fig 3b. Here we normalize each distance dd by the total number of pairs of sites that are distance dd apart. We see that, as expected for small t/Jt/J, the holes tend to be tightly bound, while for larger t/Jt/J ratios the average distance increases, suggesting more spatially separated pairs.

We probe the rotational structure of two-hole pairs by analyzing the rotational symmetry sector of the ground state. As evident from Fig. 1a, the AFM order reduces the lattice C6C_{6} symmetry to C3C_{3}. We impose this symmetry in the HFDS architecture by averaging over rotations:

|ψm3​(σ)⟩=∑i=02ei​2​π/3​j​m3​∑σψ~​(R^j​σ)​|σ⟩\ket{\psi_{m_{3}}(\sigma)}=\sum_{i=0}^{2}e^{i2\pi/3jm_{3}}\sum_{\sigma}\tilde{\psi}(\hat{R}^{j}\sigma)\ket{\sigma} (5)

where m3=0,1,2m_{3}=0,1,2 labels irreps, R^j\hat{R}^{j} rotates σ\sigma by 120∘×j120^{\circ}\times j, and ψ~\tilde{\psi} is the unsymmetrized network output. States with m3=1,2m_{3}=1,2 are degenerate due to time-reversal symmetry. To identify the symmetry sector of the unsymmetrized state, we train without symmetry constraints and use importance sampling to compute E⁡(m3)=∑s∈S~w⁡(s)​Eloc​(s)E(m_{3})=\sum_{s\in\tilde{S}}w(s)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(s), with samples S~\tilde{S} from |ψ~⟩\ket{\tilde{\psi}} and weights w⁡(s)=|ψm3​(s)|2/|ψ~​(s)|2w(s)=|\psi_{m_{3}}(s)|^{2}/|\tilde{\psi}(s)|^{2}. Results (Fig. 3c, open symbols) show that the m3=0m_{3}=0 projection has consistently higher energy than the non-trivial sectors.

We also perform fully symmetrized optimizations, which require averaging the determinants in Eq. (5), and are therefore computationally more expensive, as well as complicate the optimization for larger systems. While the optimized m3=1,2m_{3}=1,2 states have slightly lower energies, for large systems all three sectors agree within sampling error, see SM [59] for details. As a next step, further studies at finite doping will be necessary to determine the nature of a potential superconducting ground state in this regime. However, the clear result in the 3×33\times 3 system together with the suggestive data of the projection from the unsymmetrized sector presents a strong indication of a non-s-wave pairing symmetry.

Discussion and Outlook. In this work, we have investigated finite doping in the S​U​(3)SU(3) tt-JJ model on the triangular lattice. Owing to its tripartite structure, the triangular lattice with S​U​(3)SU(3)-symmetric interactions exhibits a close analogy to the much-studied S​U​(2)SU(2) bipartite square lattice. We introduced a three-flavor extension of Gutzwiller-projected hidden fermion determinant states (G-HFDS), which allows us to explore the full doping range of the S​U​(3)SU(3) triangular lattice tt-JJ model on system sizes up to 9×99\times 9 lattice sites with fully periodic boundary conditions. We analyzed two- and three-point magnetic correlations formulated in terms of the Cartan generators λ3\lambda_{3} and λ8\lambda_{8} of the S​U​(3)SU(3) group to probe the magnetic response and the nature of doped charge carriers. These observables can be directly probed in cold atom experiments [10, 62, 45] and reveal strong analogies with their counterparts on the S​U​(2)SU(2) square lattice, supporting our claim of a close correspondence between the two models.

Key phenomena such as the formation of dopant pairs, the resulting spin and charge ordering or the formation of a pseudogap may differ significantly in the S​U​(3)SU(3) case. The increased connectivity of the triangular lattice, together with the enlarged local Hilbert space due to the third spin flavor, introduces new complexity into the problem of understanding stripe formation and other forms of charge or spin order. As a first step toward addressing these questions, we examined binding energies across different parameter regimes and found values significantly above those observed in the S​U​(2)SU(2) model, suggesting an enhanced tendency for pairing. This is further supported by our analysis of hole–hole distances in the variational wavefunction, where we observe a clear crossover from tightly bound holes at low t/Jt/J to more delocalized behavior at larger t/Jt/J. We further examined the rotational symmetry of two doped holes, finding a strong indication of a non-s-wave rotational ground state. However, the detailed structure of such bound states and their implications for emergent phases remain open questions. In particular, the nature of two-particle pairing is intrinsically richer in the S​U​(3)SU(3) model due to the additional spin flavor [53] as well as the absence of particle-hole symmetry.

Our results represent an important first step toward understanding finite doping in S​U​(N)SU(N) Fermi-Hubbard models, opening a path to exploring doped Mott insulators in higher-symmetry systems beyond the S​U​(2)SU(2) paradigm and establishing a universal approach to strongly coupled systems. Our work is directly relevant to current and near-future quantum simulation experiments with ultracold alkaline-earth atoms, where S​U​(N)SU(N) symmetries naturally emerge due to the decoupling of nuclear spin from electronic degrees of freedom. In particular, quantum gas microscopy platforms offering site-resolved imaging and control can enable direct measurement of spin and charge correlations in ultracold S​U​(N)SU(N) systems [62, 21].

Code availability. Our implementation of G-HFDS is based on the NetKet package [netket3:2022], specifically https://netket.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/lattice-fermions.html and can be found on https://github.com/annikaboehler/SU3_GHFDS#.
